generation.hypothesis: High-entropy alloys with specific compositions and processing routes can exhibit high thermal stability and superior resistance to radiation damage, making them suitable for lattice heat conductivity applications.

generation.mechanism: Irradiation-induced ballistic mixing, Order-Disorder Transition Temperature (ODTT), and high interstitial-vacancy recombination rates contribute to the high irradiation resistance and thermal stability of the high-entropy alloys. falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If the high-entropy alloy exhibits significant degradation in thermal conductivity and radiation resistance under extreme irradiation environments, the hypothesis is falsified.

Question: How can a quinary refractory high-entropy alloy (RHEA) be designed to exhibit high thermal stability and superior resistance to radiation damage (dislocation loops, cavities, and grain growth) under extreme irradiation environments compared to existing quaternary W-based alloys?. System: Quinary W-Ta-Cr-V-Hf RHEA with compositions W29.4Ta42Cr5.0V16.1Hf7.5 (thin film) and W31Ta34Cr5.0V27Hf3.0 (thick film). Processing: Magnetron-sputtering deposition from metal targets (99.99% purity) at room temperature and 3 mTorr pressure with no bias voltage; power settings: W (200 W), Ta (400 W), Cr (50 W), V (350 W), Hf (25 W); film thicknesses: 100 nm (thin) and 3 µm (thick).
